newsitem.title: PERU: Japanese ashamed how reception turned to nightmare.
newsitem.headline: Japanese ashamed how reception turned to nightmare.

text.p: Displaying their traditional etiquette, Japanese diplomats held inside their embassy residence in Peru are deeply ashamed that their elegant cocktail reception turned into a nightmare.

Ambassador Morihisa Aoki, host of the ill-fated celebration, felt so bad about his 600 guests turning into hostages that he told colleagues he would resign immediately once the siege ends, released hostages told Reuters.

"When I return to Japan I will surrender my job," one quoted Aoki as telling a colleague inside the besieged residence. The hostage asked not to be identified because of the sensitivity of Aoki's comments.
Aoki and about 140 fellow hostages were still being held inside the residence on Tuesday, a week after Marxist guerrillas stormed a reception and took the guests prisoner.

Aoki, 58, and his fellow diplomats felt particular shame that the man in whose honour they hosted the reception, Japanese Emperor Akihito, was forced to cancel all public celebrations of his birthday because of the crisis.
"For the emperor to have to do this because of what happened here is dreadful," hostages quoted one Japanese diplomat as telling colleagues.

Hoping to limit damage at the start of the crisis, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto blamed Peruvian security lapses rather than Japanese blunders for the storming of the residence by around 20 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.
"If a terrorist group intrudes, it is the responsibility of the country that is guarding outside. ... If such an incident occurs in Japan, it would be Japan's responsibility," he said.

Speaking with one another inside the besieged residence, Japanese diplomats speculated that the palatial building, technically Japanese territory, would be demolished once the crisis ended because its diplomatic immunity had been so cruelly violated.

Famous as a gracious, charming host, Aoki moved continually among the hostages, joking that his party had lasted long than expected and asking if there was anything they needed. He also won praise from the captives for standing up during the initial rebel attack as bullets flew in all directions to beg the guerrillas to stop firing.
